source_batch.unit_label: CB Module D unit 1: management of foreign exchange reserves (courseware unit 11)

facts.statement: Objectives, legal framework and risk management (courseware): the guiding objectives of foreign exchange reserve management in India are like those of many central banks: safety and liquidity constitute the twin objectives of reserve management in the country, while return optimisation is kept in view within this framework. The demands on reserves vary widely depending on the exchange rate regime, the openness of the economy, the size of the external sector in GDP and the nature of markets. The level of foreign exchange reserves is an indicator of the comfort level a country enjoys in meeting its international obligations in terms of payment for imports; reserves provide a cushion against external shocks; the volatility of some of the capital flows needs reserves; it is true that reserves are not required to meet transactions motive which is to be taken care of by changes that will naturally occur in the market determined exchange rates; but in a period of transition, when structural shifts can release strong excess demand or throw up temporary bottlenecks, reserves smoothen the process of change and mitigate the pains of adjustment. Legal framework: the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 provides the overarching legal framework for deployment of reserves in different foreign currency assets and gold within the broad parameters of currencies, instruments, issuers, and counterparties; the essential legal framework for reserve management is provided in sub-sections 17(6A), 17(12), 17(12A), 17(13) and 33 (6) of the Act; in brief, the law broadly permits investment of foreign exchange reserves in specified categories like deposits with other central banks and the BIS, deposits with commercial banks overseas, debt instruments representing sovereign/sovereign-guaranteed liability with residual maturity for the debt papers not exceeding 10 years, other instruments/institutions as approved by the Central Board of the Reserve Bank in accordance with the provisions of the Act. Risk management: the broad strategy for reserve management including currency composition and investment policy is decided in consultation with the Government of India; the risk management functions are aimed at ensuring development of sound governance structure in line with the best international practices, improved accountability, a culture of risk awareness across all operations, efficient allocation of resources and development of in-house skills and expertise; the risks attendant on deployment of reserves are credit risk, market risk, liquidity risk and operational risk and the systems employed to manage these risks. Credit risk: the Reserve Bank is sensitive to the credit risk it faces on account of the investment of foreign exchange reserves in the international markets; the Reserve Bank investments in bonds/treasury bills represent debt obligations of highly rated sovereigns, central banks, and supranational entities; further, deposits are placed with central banks, the BIS and commercial banks overseas; the RBI has framed requisite guidelines for selection of issuers/counterparties with a view to enhancing the safety and liquidity aspects of the reserves; the Reserve Bank continues to apply stringent criteria for selection of counterparties; credit exposure vis-a-vis sanctioned limits in respect of approved counterparties is monitored continuously; the basic objective of such an on-going exercise is to assess whether any counterparty credit quality is under potential threat. Market risk: market risk of a multi-currency portfolio represents the potential change in valuations that result from movements in financial market prices, for example, in interest rates, foreign exchange rates, equity prices and commodity prices; the major sources of market risk for central banks are currency risk, interest rate risk and movement in gold prices; gains/losses on valuation of FCA and gold due to movements in market prices and/or prices of gold are booked under a balance sheet head named the Currency and Gold Revaluation Account (CGRA); the balances in CGRA provide a buffer against exchange rate/gold price fluctuations; the dated foreign securities are valued at market prices as on the last business day of each week and month and the appreciation/depreciation arising therefrom is transferred to the Investment Revaluation Account (IRA); the balance in IRA is meant to provide cushion against changes in the security prices over the holding period. Currency risk: arises due to movements in the exchange rates; decisions are taken on the long-term exposure to different currencies, depending on the likely movements in exchange rates and other considerations in the medium and long-term; the decision-making procedure is supported by reviews of the strategy on a regular basis. Interest rate risk: the crucial aspect of the management of interest rate risk is to protect the value of the investments as much as possible from adverse impact of interest rate movements; the interest rate sensitivity of the portfolio is identified in terms of the benchmark duration and the permitted deviation from the benchmark. Liquidity risk: the risk of not being able to sell an instrument or close a position when required without facing significant costs; it is imperative to ensure that the reserves are always highly liquid in order to be able to meet any unforeseen and emergency needs; any adverse development on the external front would pose a demand on forex reserves and, hence, the investment strategy needs a highly liquid portfolio; the choice of instruments determines the liquidity of the portfolio; for example, in some markets, treasury securities could be liquidated in large volumes without much distortion of the price in the market and, thus, can be considered as liquid; except fixed deposits with the BIS/commercial banks overseas / central banks and securities issued by supranational, almost all other types of investments are highly liquid instruments which could be converted into cash at short notice; the Reserve Bank closely monitors the portion of the reserves which could be converted into cash at a very short notice.

Operational risk, transparency and recent movements (courseware): operational risk and control system: in tune with the global trend, close attention is paid to strengthen the operational risk control arrangements; key operational procedures are documented; internally, there is total separation of the front office, and the back-office functions and the internal control systems ensure several checks at the stages of deal capture, deal processing and settlement; the deal processing and settlement, including generation of payment instructions, is also subject to internal control guidelines; there is a system of concurrent audit for monitoring compliance in respect of the internal control guidelines; further, reconciliation of accounts is done regularly; in addition to internal audit and independent monitoring, the financial accounts are audited by external statutory auditors; there is a comprehensive reporting mechanism covering significant areas of activity/operations relating to reserve management; the Reserve Bank uses SWIFT as the messaging platform to settle its trades and send financial messages to its counterparties, custodians of securities and other business partners; international best practices with respect to usage and security of SWIFT system are followed; all the necessary upgrades were timely implemented in the SWIFT Alliance Access system along with strict compliance with all the mandatory security control measures as recommended by SWIFT. Transparency and disclosures: the Reserve Bank has been making available in the public domain data relating to Foreign Exchange Reserves, its operations in foreign exchange market, position of the country external assets and liabilities and earnings from deployment of Foreign Currency Assets and gold through periodic press releases of its Weekly Statistical Supplements, Monthly Bulletins, Annual Reports, etc.; the Reserve Bank approach regarding transparency and disclosure closely follows international best practices in this regard; the Reserve Bank has adopted the Special Data Dissemination Standards (SDDS) template of the IMF for publication of the detailed data on Foreign Exchange Reserves; such data are made available on monthly basis on the Reserve Bank website. Recent developments: the Reserve Bank of India publishes half-yearly reports on management of foreign exchange reserves as part of its efforts towards enhanced transparency and levels of disclosure; these reports are prepared half yearly with reference to the position as at end-March and end-September each year; the present report is with reference to the position as at end-March 2022. Composition: as on March 2022 total foreign exchange reserves were reported to the tune of USD 607,309 million; Table 11.1 gives the movement during September 2021 to March 2022; the components are the Foreign Currency Assets (FCA), gold, Special Drawing Rights (SDR) and the Reserve Tranche Position (RTP) in the International Monetary Fund (IMF); notes: FCA are maintained as a multi-currency portfolio comprising major currencies, such as US dollar, Euro, Pound sterling, Japanese yen, etc. and are valued in terms of US dollars; FCA excludes (i) investment in bonds issued by IIFC (UK) (ii) SDR holdings of Reserve Bank, which is included under SDR and (c) amount lent under SAARC Swap Arrangement; the Reserve Tranche Position is the difference between the International Monetary Fund holdings of that country currency and the country IMF-designated quota. Although both US dollar and Euro are intervention currencies and the Foreign Currency Assets (FCA) are maintained in major currencies, the foreign exchange reserves are denominated and expressed in US dollar terms; movements in the FCA occur mainly on account of purchase and sale of foreign exchange by the RBI, income arising out of the deployment of the foreign exchange reserves, external aid receipts of the Central Government and changes on account of revaluation of the assets. Sources of accretion: the sources of variation in foreign exchange reserves include the current account balance, capital account (net) (foreign investment (FDI, portfolio investment), banking capital (including NRI deposits), short term credit, external assistance, external commercial borrowings, other items in capital account) and valuation changes; on a balance of payments basis (excluding valuation effects) foreign exchange reserves increased by USD 4.6 billion during April-June 2022 as compared with USD 31.9 billion during April-June 2021; foreign exchange reserves in nominal terms (including valuation effects) decreased by USD 18.2 billion during April-June 2022 as against an increase of USD 34.1 billion in the corresponding period of the preceding year; the valuation loss, reflecting the appreciation of the US dollar against major currencies, amounted to USD 22.7 billion during April-June 2022 as against a valuation gain of USD 2.2 billion during April-June 2021. Forward outstanding: the net forward asset (receivable) of the Reserve Bank in domestic foreign exchange market stood at USD 68.20 billion as at the end of March 2021. External liabilities vis-a-vis foreign exchange reserves: India International Investment Position (IIP) is a summary record of the stock of country external financial assets and liabilities; during the period between end-March 2021 and end-March 2022, the external assets increased by USD 61.1 billion and external liabilities increased by USD 65.8 billion; net IIP decreased by USD 4.6 billion; the net IIP at end-March 2022 was negative at USD 359.8 billion against a negative net IIP of USD 355.2 billion at end-March 2021, implying that the stock of all external liabilities is more than that of external assets in both periods; the ratio of India international financial assets to international financial liabilities increased to 71.9 per cent in March 2022 from 70.8 per cent a year earlier; the share of debt liabilities in total external liabilities increased marginally to 49.2 per cent at end-March 2022 from 48.5 per cent a quarter ago.

Adequacy of reserves, gold and other aspects (courseware): adequacy of reserves: at end of December 2021, foreign exchange reserves cover of imports (on balance of payments basis) declined to 13.1 months from 14.6 months at end-September 2021; the ratio of short-term debt (original maturity) to reserves, which was 16.5 per cent at end-September 2021, increased to 18.1 per cent at end-December 2021; the ratio of volatile capital flows (including cumulative portfolio inflows and outstanding short-term debt) to reserves increased from 64.1 per cent at end-September 2021 to 65.0 per cent at end-December 2021. Quarterly variations: net claims of non-residents on India increased by US$ 5.6 billion during Q4:2021-22 to US$ 359.8 billion in March 2022; this rise in net claims was due to larger decline in the Indian residents overseas financial assets (US$ (-)7.3 billion) when compared to the decline in foreign-owned assets in India (US$ (-)1.7 billion); the foreign assets of Indian residents declined during Q4:2021-22, mainly due to a decrease of US$ 26.3 billion in reserve assets even as direct, portfolio and other investments, such as trade credits and currency and deposits increased during the period; even though reserve assets declined during the quarter, it accounted for around two thirds of India international financial assets; variation in the exchange rate of rupee vis-a-vis other currencies had a significant impact on the change in liabilities, when valued in US$ terms, as the rupee depreciated by 2.02 per cent during the quarter; the share of debt liabilities in total external liabilities increased marginally to 49.2 per cent. Annual variations: during 2021-22, non-residents net claims on India increased by US$ 4.6 billion; increase in foreign owned assets in India (US$ 65.8 billion) exceeded the rise in overseas assets of Indian residents (US$ 61.1 billion); international financial assets of Indian residents increased primarily due to increase in reserve assets (US$ 30.3 billion), direct investment (US$ 17.7 billion) and trade credits (US$ 13.0 billion); in spite of a decline of US$ 16.1 billion in portfolio investment during the financial year, international financial liabilities increased on the back of large rise in direct investment in India (US$ 39.6 billion) and other investments (US$ 42.4 billion); the ratio of India international financial assets to international financial liabilities increased to 71.9 per cent in March 2022 from 70.8 per cent a year earlier. Management of gold reserves: as at end-March 2022, the Reserve Bank held 760.42 metric tonnes of gold (including gold deposits of 11.08 metric tonnes); during which 453.52 metric tonnes of gold is held overseas in safe custody with the Bank of England and the Bank for International Settlements (BIS); 295.82 metric tonnes of gold is held domestically; in value terms (USD), the share of gold in the total foreign exchange reserves increased from about 5.88 per cent at end-September 2021 to about 7.01 per cent at end-March 2022. Investment pattern of foreign currency assets: the foreign currency assets comprise multi-currency assets that are held in multi-asset portfolios as per the existing norms, which conform to the best international practices followed in this regard; as at end-March 2022, out of the total FCA of USD 540.72 billion, USD 363.03 billion was invested in securities, USD 140.54 billion was deposited with other central banks and the BIS and the balance USD 37.16 billion comprised deposits with commercial banks overseas (securities 67.14 per cent, deposits with other central banks and BIS 25.99 per cent, deposits with commercial banks overseas 6.87 per cent). Other related aspects: the Financial Transaction Plan (FTP) of the IMF: during the half year under review (September 2021-March 2022), there were two Purchase Transactions aggregating USD 172.15 million and two repurchase transactions aggregating USD 22.56 million under the FTP of the IMF. Investments under New Arrangements to Borrow (NAB) and Note Purchase Agreement (NPA) with IMF: India has committed to provide resources up to SDR 4,440.91 million under the IMF New Arrangements to Borrow (NAB); effective January 01, 2021, the size of IMF NAB has been doubled; India commitment under NAB now stands at SDR 8,881.82 million as on March 31, 2022; RBI has subscribed to Notes equivalent to SDR 88.62 million under NAB till the end of March 2022, as part of Government of India Contribution; in terms of the Note Purchase Agreement (NPA) 2020, entered into between RBI and IMF, RBI has agreed to invest an amount equivalent to USD 3.90 billion in SDR denominated Notes issued by IMF. SAARC Swap Arrangements: Bhutan availed a swap of Rs 14,541.94 million equivalent to USD 200 million on March 15, 2021, due for maturity on June 15, 2021; the swap was rolled over twice for three months each; Maldives availed a swap of USD 250 million on December 29, 2020 for six months; Sri Lanka availed a swap of USD 400 million on January 13, 2022 for three months with maturity falling on April 18, 2022. Investment in bonds issued by IIFC (UK): the Reserve Bank has the mandate to invest up to USD 5 billion in the bonds issued by the India Infrastructure Finance Company (UK) Limited; as at end-March 2022, the amount invested in such bonds stood at USD 1.44 billion. Summing up: the level of foreign exchange reserves is an indicator of the comfort level a country enjoys in meeting its international obligations in terms of payment for imports; present level of foreign exchange reserves is a source of comfort as it provides a measure of insulation against unforeseen external shocks or shocks created by domestic supply shortages; it also helps to meet the precautionary motive and satisfy the need for liquidity, which instils confidence in the Indian economy among international investors and financial markets; the Reserve Bank is prudently trying to stabilise Rupee by selling US Dollar given its strengthening on-going war between Ukraine and Russia from February 2022 onwards; India total foreign exchange (Forex) reserves stood at around USD 532.838 Billion as on 07 Oct 2022, with the Foreign Exchange Assets (FCA) component at around US$ 471.496 Billion, Gold Reserves at around US$38.995 Billion, SDRs (Special Drawing Rights with the IMF) of around US$ 17.582 Billion.

payload.title: Objectives, legal framework and the four risks in reserve management
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Objectives:** **safety and liquidity** are the **twin objectives**; **return optimisation** is sought **within** those limits. The demand for reserves depends on the **exchange rate regime**, **openness**, the **size of the external sector** and **market depth**.

**Why hold reserves:** they show **comfort in meeting international obligations (import payments)** and give a **cushion against external shocks** and **volatile capital flows**. The **transactions motive** is largely met by a **market-determined exchange rate**, but in **transition** reserves **smooth adjustment** and give **additional comfort**.

**Legal framework:** the **RBI Act, 1934** (**Sections 17(6A), 17(12), 17(12A), 17(13) and 33(6)**) permits **deposits with the BIS and other central banks**, **deposits with commercial banks abroad**, **sovereign or sovereign-guaranteed debt with residual maturity up to 10 years**, and other instruments approved by the **Central Board**. Currency composition and investment policy are set **in consultation with the Government**.

**Risks and controls:**

| Risk | Management |
| --- | --- |
| **Credit** | **Highly rated sovereigns, central banks, supranationals**; deposits with **central banks, the BIS, commercial banks**; **counterparty selection guidelines** and **continuous limit monitoring** |
| **Market** | **Currency, interest rate and gold price** risk; gains and losses booked in the **Currency and Gold Revaluation Account (CGRA)**; **dated securities** valued at **market prices weekly and monthly** with changes going to the **Investment Revaluation Account (IRA)** as a **buffer** |
| **Currency** | Long-term **exposure decisions** reviewed regularly |
| **Interest rate** | **Benchmark duration** and **permitted deviation** |
| **Liquidity** | Portfolio kept **highly liquid** (Treasury securities can be sold in size; **fixed deposits** and **supranational** paper are less liquid); the portion convertible into cash at **short notice** is monitored |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Reserves must be safe and liquid first, with returns a secondary aim.

self_check.prompt_text: Which two objectives guide the management of India's foreign exchange reserves?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Safety and liquidity, with return optimisation within that framework.

payload.title: Operational risk, transparency, composition and sources of variation
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Operational risk controls:** **documented procedures**, **separation of front office and back office**, checks at **deal capture, processing and settlement**, **concurrent audit**, **regular reconciliation**, **internal and external audit**, and **SWIFT** (Alliance Access) with strict **security controls**.

**Transparency:** data are published in **Weekly Statistical Supplements, Monthly Bulletins, Annual Reports** and **press releases**; the Reserve Bank follows the IMF **Special Data Dissemination Standards (SDDS)** template, with **monthly** data on its website, and publishes a **half-yearly report** on reserve management (positions at **end-March and end-September**).

**Composition:** **Foreign Currency Assets (FCA)** (a **multi-currency portfolio** valued in **US dollars**; it **excludes** investment in **IIFC (UK)** bonds, **SDR** holdings and amounts lent under the **SAARC swap**), **gold**, **SDRs** and the **Reserve Tranche Position (RTP)** (the **difference between the IMF's holdings of a member's currency and its quota**). Reserves are **expressed in US dollars**; **FCA movements** come from **purchases and sales of foreign exchange**, **income from deployment**, **external aid receipts** and **revaluation**.

**Sources of variation:** the **current account balance**; the **capital account** (**FDI and portfolio investment**, **banking capital including NRI deposits**, **short-term credit**, **external assistance**, **ECBs**, others); and **valuation changes**. On a **BoP basis** (excluding valuation) reserves rose **USD 4.6 billion in April-June 2022**, but **including a USD 22.7 billion valuation loss** (a stronger US dollar) they **fell USD 18.2 billion**.

**Forward book:** the **net forward asset** of the Reserve Bank in the domestic market was **USD 68.20 billion at end-March 2021**.

**International Investment Position (IIP):** the **stock of external assets and liabilities**; the **net IIP is negative** (about **USD 359.8 billion at end-March 2022**), and the **assets-to-liabilities ratio** was about **71.9 per cent**; **debt liabilities** were about **49.2 per cent** of external liabilities.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Valuation changes can swamp transaction flows in the movement of reserves.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the Reserve Tranche Position?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The difference between the IMF holdings of a country currency and the country IMF-designated quota.

payload.title: Adequacy of reserves, gold, deployment of FCA and other aspects
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Adequacy indicators (December 2021):** **import cover** fell to **13.1 months** (from **14.6** in September 2021); **short-term debt (original maturity) to reserves** rose from **16.5 to 18.1 per cent**; **volatile capital flows to reserves** rose from **64.1 to 65.0 per cent**. Reserve assets are about **two thirds of India's international financial assets**.

**Variation:** over **2021-22** **foreign-owned assets in India rose by USD 65.8 billion**, more than the **USD 61.1 billion rise in residents' overseas assets**, so **net claims of non-residents rose by USD 4.6 billion**; **exchange rate changes** (the **rupee depreciated about 2 per cent** in the quarter) affect **liabilities valued in US dollars**.

**Gold:** the Reserve Bank's holding at **end-March 2022** was **760.42 tonnes** (**453.52 tonnes abroad** with the **Bank of England and the BIS**, **295.82 tonnes domestic**); the **gold share of reserves** rose from about **5.88 to 7.01 per cent**.

**Deployment of FCA (March 2022):** about **67 per cent in securities**, **26 per cent placed with other central banks and the BIS** and **7 per cent placed with commercial banks abroad**.

**Other items:** the IMF **Financial Transaction Plan** (purchases and repurchases), **New Arrangements to Borrow (NAB)** (India's commitment doubled from **1 January 2021**) and the **Note Purchase Agreement**; **SAARC swap arrangements** (Bhutan, Maldives, Sri Lanka); the Reserve Bank may invest up to **USD 5 billion** in bonds of the **India Infrastructure Finance Company (UK)**.

**Summing up:** reserves are a **comfort level** and **insulation** from external shocks, meet **precautionary** needs and build **confidence**; the Reserve Bank sold dollars to stabilise the rupee after **February 2022**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Adequacy is judged against imports, short-term debt and volatile flows.

self_check.expected_takeaway: With the Bank of England and the Bank for International Settlements.

items.title: Objectives, legal framework and the four risks in reserve management
items.core_explanation_md:
**Objectives:** **safety and liquidity** are the **twin objectives**; **return optimisation** is sought **within** those limits. The demand for reserves depends on the **exchange rate regime**, **openness**, the **size of the external sector** and **market depth**.

**Why hold reserves:** they show **comfort in meeting international obligations (import payments)** and give a **cushion against external shocks** and **volatile capital flows**. The **transactions motive** is largely met by a **market-determined exchange rate**, but in **transition** reserves **smooth adjustment** and give **additional comfort**.

**Legal framework:** the **RBI Act, 1934** (**Sections 17(6A), 17(12), 17(12A), 17(13) and 33(6)**) permits **deposits with the BIS and other central banks**, **deposits with commercial banks abroad**, **sovereign or sovereign-guaranteed debt with residual maturity up to 10 years**, and other instruments approved by the **Central Board**. Currency composition and investment policy are set **in consultation with the Government**.

**Risks and controls:**

| Risk | Management |
| --- | --- |
| **Credit** | **Highly rated sovereigns, central banks, supranationals**; deposits with **central banks, the BIS, commercial banks**; **counterparty selection guidelines** and **continuous limit monitoring** |
| **Market** | **Currency, interest rate and gold price** risk; gains and losses booked in the **Currency and Gold Revaluation Account (CGRA)**; **dated securities** valued at **market prices weekly and monthly** with changes going to the **Investment Revaluation Account (IRA)** as a **buffer** |
| **Currency** | Long-term **exposure decisions** reviewed regularly |
| **Interest rate** | **Benchmark duration** and **permitted deviation** |
| **Liquidity** | Portfolio kept **highly liquid** (Treasury securities can be sold in size; **fixed deposits** and **supranational** paper are less liquid); the portion convertible into cash at **short notice** is monitored |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Reserves must be safe and liquid first, with returns a secondary aim.

items.title: Operational risk, transparency, composition and sources of variation
items.core_explanation_md:
**Operational risk controls:** **documented procedures**, **separation of front office and back office**, checks at **deal capture, processing and settlement**, **concurrent audit**, **regular reconciliation**, **internal and external audit**, and **SWIFT** (Alliance Access) with strict **security controls**.

**Transparency:** data are published in **Weekly Statistical Supplements, Monthly Bulletins, Annual Reports** and **press releases**; the Reserve Bank follows the IMF **Special Data Dissemination Standards (SDDS)** template, with **monthly** data on its website, and publishes a **half-yearly report** on reserve management (positions at **end-March and end-September**).

**Composition:** **Foreign Currency Assets (FCA)** (a **multi-currency portfolio** valued in **US dollars**; it **excludes** investment in **IIFC (UK)** bonds, **SDR** holdings and amounts lent under the **SAARC swap**), **gold**, **SDRs** and the **Reserve Tranche Position (RTP)** (the **difference between the IMF's holdings of a member's currency and its quota**). Reserves are **expressed in US dollars**; **FCA movements** come from **purchases and sales of foreign exchange**, **income from deployment**, **external aid receipts** and **revaluation**.

**Sources of variation:** the **current account balance**; the **capital account** (**FDI and portfolio investment**, **banking capital including NRI deposits**, **short-term credit**, **external assistance**, **ECBs**, others); and **valuation changes**. On a **BoP basis** (excluding valuation) reserves rose **USD 4.6 billion in April-June 2022**, but **including a USD 22.7 billion valuation loss** (a stronger US dollar) they **fell USD 18.2 billion**.

**Forward book:** the **net forward asset** of the Reserve Bank in the domestic market was **USD 68.20 billion at end-March 2021**.

**International Investment Position (IIP):** the **stock of external assets and liabilities**; the **net IIP is negative** (about **USD 359.8 billion at end-March 2022**), and the **assets-to-liabilities ratio** was about **71.9 per cent**; **debt liabilities** were about **49.2 per cent** of external liabilities.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Valuation changes can swamp transaction flows in the movement of reserves.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The difference between the IMF holdings of a country currency and the country IMF-designated quota.

items.title: Adequacy of reserves, gold, deployment of FCA and other aspects
items.core_explanation_md:
**Adequacy indicators (December 2021):** **import cover** fell to **13.1 months** (from **14.6** in September 2021); **short-term debt (original maturity) to reserves** rose from **16.5 to 18.1 per cent**; **volatile capital flows to reserves** rose from **64.1 to 65.0 per cent**. Reserve assets are about **two thirds of India's international financial assets**.

**Variation:** over **2021-22** **foreign-owned assets in India rose by USD 65.8 billion**, more than the **USD 61.1 billion rise in residents' overseas assets**, so **net claims of non-residents rose by USD 4.6 billion**; **exchange rate changes** (the **rupee depreciated about 2 per cent** in the quarter) affect **liabilities valued in US dollars**.

**Gold:** the Reserve Bank's holding at **end-March 2022** was **760.42 tonnes** (**453.52 tonnes abroad** with the **Bank of England and the BIS**, **295.82 tonnes domestic**); the **gold share of reserves** rose from about **5.88 to 7.01 per cent**.

**Deployment of FCA (March 2022):** about **67 per cent in securities**, **26 per cent placed with other central banks and the BIS** and **7 per cent placed with commercial banks abroad**.

**Other items:** the IMF **Financial Transaction Plan** (purchases and repurchases), **New Arrangements to Borrow (NAB)** (India's commitment doubled from **1 January 2021**) and the **Note Purchase Agreement**; **SAARC swap arrangements** (Bhutan, Maldives, Sri Lanka); the Reserve Bank may invest up to **USD 5 billion** in bonds of the **India Infrastructure Finance Company (UK)**.

**Summing up:** reserves are a **comfort level** and **insulation** from external shocks, meet **precautionary** needs and build **confidence**; the Reserve Bank sold dollars to stabilise the rupee after **February 2022**.
